etymology: Hebrew Erek, of uncertain meaning (some read “length”); one of the cities of the beginning of Nimrod’s kingdom in the land of Shinar, the Uruk of the plain.
biblical_def: Erech stands second in the roll of Nimrod’s first cities: “And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar” (Gen 10:10). Here on the plain of Shinar, the same plain where men said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower whose top may reach unto heaven, rose the first empire of the world. Nimrod was a mighty hunter before the LORD, and the beginning of his kingdom was Babel and her sister cities. Erech was thus a stone in the first monument of man’s self-exaltation, the kingdom of the earth set up over against the kingdom of God. Yet even this the LORD ruled and overruled, for He made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth, and determined the times before appointed and the bounds of their habitation (Act 17:26). The heathen rage and the people imagine a vain thing (Psa 2:1); the towers of Shinar rise and fall; but the counsel of the LORD standeth for ever. And out of these scattered nations He drew forth Abram, and promised, In thee shall all families of the earth be blessed (Gen 12:3). Erech built for man’s glory; God builds a city for His own, and the gates of Babel shall not prevail against it.
webster_summary: One of the first cities of Nimrod’s kingdom in the land of Shinar (Gen 10:10); a stone in the first empire of man’s self-exaltation, ruled and overruled by the sovereign LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Akkad, of uncertain meaning; a city of Nimrod in the land of Shinar that lent its name to the Akkadian realm of the eastern plain.
biblical_def: Third in Nimrod’s roll of cities stands Accad, in the land of Shinar (Gen 10:10). Nimrod is called a mighty hunter before the LORD, and the phrase is no praise but a warning, for his might was turned to dominion, and the beginning of his kingdom was a cluster of cities raised on the plain of rebellion. Accad lent its name to a mighty realm, yet mightiness of the arm of flesh is a small thing in the sight of heaven. Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance (Isa 40:15). The LORD who sitteth upon the circle of the earth takes up the isles as a very little thing, and the kingdoms that men build to their own name He weighs and finds wanting. Against Nimrod’s kingdom of the hunter God set His own King: Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession (Psa 2:8). Earthly dominion built in rebellion cannot stand, but the dominion of the Son endures. And to the seed of Abram came the word that turns the empire on its head: In thee shall all families of the earth be blessed (Gen 12:3). Accad sought greatness by conquest; the meek inherit the earth by grace.
webster_summary: A city of Nimrod in the land of Shinar (Gen 10:10) that named the Akkadian realm; a witness to the vanity of dominion built by the arm of flesh in rebellion against God.

corruption_paragraphs: Accad is a name of the deep past, a city and then an empire on the plain of Shinar. The modern world contests nothing about it, and the text asks no defence, only reading: the mighty hunter built his kingdom, and it is numbered with the dust.

etymology: Hebrew Kalneh; a city of Nimrod’s kingdom in the land of Shinar, named again by the prophet Amos as a byword of vanished greatness.
biblical_def: Calneh closes the list of the first cities of Nimrod’s kingdom in Shinar (Gen 10:10), and centuries later the prophet Amos names her again as a warning to the careless in Zion: “Pass ye unto Calneh, and see…be they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border?” (Amo 6:2). The word cut two ways. To Israel at ease it said, You are no safer than the great cities that have fallen; and to the nations it said, Your greatness is no shield. Calneh became a byword of vanished glory, a city whose name outlived her walls only as a lesson. All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity (Isa 40:17). The greatness of the peoples is weighed in the LORD’s balance and found no better than Israel under judgment, for He is no respecter of persons and levels every human pride. The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted (Psa 46:6). Calneh preaches the end of all boasting. Whether a man trust in the ramparts of Shinar or in the temple of Jerusalem, only the LORD is a sure defence; and the city that abides is the one whose builder and maker is God.

corruption_paragraphs: Calneh raises no dispute in the present age; she is a ruin and a proverb. The corruption she rebukes is older than any theory, the ancient boast of the strong city that thinks its walls a match for heaven.

etymology: Hebrew Resen, perhaps “bridle” or “fountain-head”; the great city built between Nineveh and Calah in the northward spread of Asshur’s land.
biblical_def: Of Resen alone among these cities the Scripture pauses to say, “the same is a great city” (Gen 10:12). It lay between Nineveh and Calah, in the northward spread of the kingdom when out of the land of Shinar went forth Asshur and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah (Gen 10:11). Great in the eyes of men, Resen has left not a stone that men can surely name; her greatness is a word in a genealogy and no more. So passes the glory of the great cities of the earth. The nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance (Isa 40:15); the LORD taketh up the isles as a very little thing. Yet the same God who lets the cities of the mighty crumble is He who made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Act 17:26). Man builds and names his city great; the LORD reigns, and appoints its rise and its appointed end. Resen is a monument to the vanity of earthly greatness and a witness that the times and the bounds of every people rest not in Nimrod’s hand but in the hand of God.

etymology: Hebrew Seba; the firstborn of the sons of Cush and the people sprung from him, a nation of the far south named ever with Ethiopia.
biblical_def: Seba was the firstborn of the sons of Cush (Gen 10:7), and the people sprung from him dwelt in the far south, named ever with Ethiopia. Their glory in Scripture is not their own but the King’s to whom they are given. In the great psalm of Solomon’s greater Son it is written, “The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts” (Psa 72:10). And in the mouth of the LORD Himself Seba becomes a ransom-price for His beloved: “I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee” (Isa 43:3). Here is a deep mercy, that God so values His redeemed He speaks of whole nations as the price He is willing to give for them, a shadow of that unspeakable price, the precious blood of Christ, by which a people out of every nation is bought. Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God (Psa 68:31). The kings of the far south, once outside the covenant, are seen bowing to the throne of David’s Son and bringing their tribute. Seba the son of Cush thus preaches the gathering of the nations to Christ, the ransomed become the worshippers, the tributary made a willing subject of the King of kings.
webster_summary: The firstborn son of Cush and his people (Gen 10:7), named by God as a ransom-price and a tributary to the King (Isa 43:3; Psa 72:10); a figure of the nations gathered to Christ.

etymology: Hebrew Sabtah; the third of the sons of Cush and father of an Arabian people of the eastern desert.
biblical_def: Sabtah is named without a story, the third of the sons of Cush (Gen 10:7), father of an Arabian people of the eastern desert. Scripture records his name and passes on, yet the naming itself is doctrine. The sons of Ham are set down man by man — Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan (Gen 10:6) — and their sons after them, that no people might think itself sprung from the earth or from chance. The LORD reckons every nation from one man, and hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Act 17:26). There is no tribe beyond the map of His providence, no desert people forgotten in His book. Sabtah’s obscure sons were as surely appointed their times and their borders as the great nations whose wars fill the histories. And the God who numbers them is the living God, not one of the vain idols the nations serve: For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens (Psa 96:5). The name Sabtah, kept in the sacred record when empires are forgotten, testifies that the least and most nameless of the peoples is known to God, and that He who counted them will gather a remnant out of them all.
webster_summary: The third son of Cush and father of an Arabian people (Gen 10:7); a witness that the LORD reckons every nation from one man and that no people lies beyond the map of His providence.

etymology: Hebrew Ra'mah, perhaps “trembling”; a son of Cush and father of Sheba and Dedan, a trading people of the spice roads.
biblical_def: Raamah, a son of Cush, was father of Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7), and the people of his name became merchants of the desert trade. When Ezekiel sang his lament over Tyre, that great mart of the nations, Raamah stood among her traffickers: “The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, they were thy merchants: they occupied in thy fairs with chief of all spices, and with all precious stones, and gold” (Eze 27:22). Here is the wealth of the nations poured into the lap of a proud city that God would humble. Yet the spices and gold of Raamah are not lost to a nobler use, for what the nations lavish on their Tyres God will one day gather into His own city. The multitude of camels shall cover thee…all they from Sheba shall come: they shall bring gold and incense; and they shall shew forth the praises of the LORD (Isa 60:6). The kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts (Psa 72:10). The merchandise of the peoples, hoarded now for mammon, shall be brought as tribute to the King whose glory fills His temple. Raamah the trader preaches that the wealth of the Gentiles is the LORD’s, and that the gold which the nations spend on vanity shall yet adorn the worship of the true and living God.

etymology: Hebrew Dedan; a caravan people of northern Arabia, sons of Raamah and near kin to the trade of Edom.
biblical_def: Dedan was a caravan people of northern Arabia, sons of Raamah (Gen 10:7) and near kin to the trade of Edom. Ezekiel names them among the merchants of Tyre: “Dedan was thy merchant in precious clothes for chariots” (Eze 27:20). But the word that most concerns their souls is the word of warning, for their dwelling lay in the shadow of the mountain of Esau, and when the calamity of Edom drew near the prophet cried, “Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time that I will visit him” (Jer 49:8). Here is the summons that comes to every trafficker of the earth who dwells too near the doomed: flee the wrath to come. The LORD hath a controversy with the nations, he will plead with all flesh; he will give them that are wicked to the sword (Jer 25:31). The caravans of Dedan pass by the falling cities, and the gospel takes up their alarm and turns it to mercy: flee, dwell deep, hide in the clefts of the Rock. The Dedanite bidden to escape the calamity of Esau is a picture of the sinner bidden to flee to Christ before the day of visitation; happy the man who heeds the cry and turns back in time.

etymology: Hebrew Put (Phut), the third son of Ham (Gen 10:6); the land and people of Libya west of Egypt, a hired soldiery of the nations.
biblical_def: Put, or Phut, was the third son of Ham (Gen 10:6), the land and people of Libya to the west of Egypt. Their trade in Scripture was war; they hired out their strength to the great powers and fell with them. In Tyre’s army they stood as mercenaries: “They of Persia and of Lud and of Phut were in thine army, thy men of war: they hanged the shield and helmet in thee; they set forth thy comeliness” (Eze 27:10). And when Nahum proclaimed the doom of No, Put was numbered among her helpers: “Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers” (Nah 3:9). Yet the helpers could not save; Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers…whose rampart was the sea? (Nah 3:8) — and No fell for all her allies. Put is the very image of the arm of flesh. The nations that lend their strength to the doomed are dragged down in the same ruin, for cursed is the man that trusteth in man and maketh flesh his arm. Better one nation whose God is the LORD than all the hired soldiery of the earth. Put preaches that no confederacy of the strong can stand against the LORD of hosts, and that the strength men sell for wages perishes with those who buy it.
webster_summary: The third son of Ham (Gen 10:6), Libya, the hired soldiery of Tyre and ally of Egypt and No (Eze 27:10; Nah 3:9); the very image of the arm of flesh that falls with the doomed it serves.

corruption_summary: Libya, the hired soldiery of the nations; it recovers the folly of trusting the arm of flesh and the ruin that falls on those who lend their strength to the doomed.
corruption_paragraphs: Put is an ancient people of North Africa, and the present age presses no redefinition upon the name. The entry recovers not a grievance but a warning as old as the prophets: the hired sword cannot save either him who wields it or him who buys it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the vanity of the arm of flesh. Put lent its strength to Tyre and to No, and fell with them both; the helpers could not turn away the day of doom. Cursed is the man that trusteth in man and maketh flesh his arm. Better one nation whose God is the LORD than all the mercenaries of the earth, for no confederacy of the strong can stand against the LORD of hosts.

etymology: Hebrew Lud; a son of Shem (Gen 10:22), a people afterward known as men of the bow among the far nations of the earth.
biblical_def: Lud is named among the sons of Shem — “Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram” (Gen 10:22) — a people afterward known as men of the bow among the far nations of the earth. They dwelt at the edge of the known world, and to such far-off peoples, who had not seen the LORD’s glory nor heard His fame, His purpose reached even in the prophets. Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else (Isa 45:22). The gospel is no narrow river bounded by Jordan, but a sea that fills the ends of the earth. “For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles…saith the LORD of hosts” (Mal 1:11). The far nations that knew not God are appointed to hear, and messengers are sent to declare His glory among them. And the end is sure, beheld already by John: “A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb” (Rev 7:9). Lud the archer, a name in an old genealogy, is a token of the peoples afar off to whom the arrows of the King are sent, that they too may bow before the Lamb.
webster_summary: A son of Shem (Gen 10:22), a people of the bow among the far nations; a token of the far-off peoples who knew not God, to whom His glory shall be declared and who shall stand before the Lamb.

corruption_paragraphs: Lud is a far and shadowy name in the table of nations, and the present age raises no quarrel over it. The entry recovers not a grievance but a commission: that the peoples at the edge of the earth are appointed to hear the LORD’s glory declared.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of the gospel to the nations afar off. Lud dwelt at the world’s edge and knew not God, yet the word runs even there: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth. From the rising of the sun to its going down His name shall be great among the Gentiles, and the end is already beheld, a multitude no man can number, of all nations and kindreds and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb.
